rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth is the country where the elder brother suffered the event that would anger his father; his wording deliberately confines him there as though in prison, to establish an excuse.
rows.anchor: أرض القطر والموضع الذي ناله فيه المكروه المؤدي إلى سخط أبيه، والمقصد بهذا اللفظ التحريج على نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s decision for him is a general expression covering any destiny that might return him, including death, victory, or fulfillment of his hope.
rows.anchor: لفظ عام بجميع ما يمكن أن يرده من القدر كالموت أو النصرة وبلوغ الأمل وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih interprets God’s judgment for the elder brother as judgment by the sword.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح: أو يحكم الله لي بالسيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb يحكم is subjunctive by coordination with يأذن; alternatively أو means إلا أن, in which case يحكم is subjunctive after أو.
rows.anchor: ونصب يحكم بالعطف على يأذن، ويجوز أن تكون أو في هذا الموضع بمعنى إلا أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob wept on their return, lamenting that each journey had cost him another son: Joseph, Simeon, then Benjamin and Reuben.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم لما وصلوا إلى يعقوب بكى وقال: يا بني ما تذهبون عني مرة إلا نقصتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to return to their father is attributed either to the eldest brother or Joseph; the first attribution is more apparent.
rows.anchor: الأمر بالرجوع قيل: هو من قول كبيرهم، وقيل: بل هو من قول يوسف لهم، والأول أظهر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The common reading treats Benjamin’s theft as established according to the outward facts.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «سرق» على تحقيق السرقة على بنيامين، بحسب ظاهر الأمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Abu Razin read the verb with a doubled consonant, expressing caution rather than conclusively accusing Benjamin; this reading is also transmitted from al-Kisa'i.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وأبو رزين «سرق» بضم السين وكسر الراء وتشديدها

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reads ابنك سارق, an indefinite ‘thief,’ and says they investigated afterward.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك: «إن ابنك سارق» بالألف وتنوين القاف، ثم تحروا بعد

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says their testimony reported only what outward events let them know; knowledge of the unseen belongs to God.
rows.anchor: والعلم في الغيب إلى الله، ليس في ذلك حفظنا، هذا قول ابن إسحاق،

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says they told Joseph that they knew his law required the thief to be retained, but could not have known theft would occur from one of their bags.
rows.anchor:
وقال ابن زيد: قولهم: ما شهدنا إلا بما علمنا أرادوا به:
وما شهدنا عند يوسف بأن السارق يسترق في شرعك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan’s reading adds عليه, specifying that their testimony was against the son only on the basis of what they knew.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن «وما شهدنا عليه إلا بما علمنا» بزيادة «عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative explanation takes الغيب to mean night in Himyarite usage: they knew the outward situation but could not guard against theft or deception occurring at night.
rows.anchor: وروي أن معنى قولهم: للغيب أي الليل، والغيب: الليل- بلغة حمير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The town they ask Jacob to question is Egypt, and town and caravan mean their inhabitants; this is the majority view and the author’s preferred reading as metaphor.
rows.anchor: وهي مصر، قاله ابن عباس وغيره، وهذا مجاز، والمراد أهلها، وكذلك قوله: والعير

rows.speaker: أبو المعالي
rows.claim: Abu al-Ma'ali reports a theologian’s view that the phrase omits a noun rather than using metaphor, since metaphor means borrowing a word for something else.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو المعالي في التلخيص عن بعض المتكلمين أنه قال: هذا من الحذف وليس من المجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says deleting an annexed noun is the essence and strongest form of metaphor according to Sibawayh and other theorists, though not every deletion is metaphorical; Abu al-Ma'ali favors metaphor here and reports it as the majority view.
rows.anchor: وحذف المضاف هو عين المجاز وعظمه- هذا مذهب سيبويه وغيره من أهل النظر- وليس كل حذف مجازا

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says the brothers literally directed Jacob to question inanimate objects and animals, which could truthfully answer a prophet.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: بل أحالوه على سؤال الجمادات والبهائم حقيقة، ومن حيث هو نبي فلا يبعد أن تخبره بالحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author considers literal questioning possible but remote, and judges the metaphorical reading stronger.
rows.anchor: وهذا وإن جوز فبعيد، والأول أقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage supplies an omitted transition after the brothers’ report: Jacob then says their souls had made the matter seem good to them.
rows.anchor: وهنا كلام مقدر يقتضيه الظاهر، تقديره: فلما قالوا هذه المقالة لأبيهم قال: بل سولت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the eldest brother’s speech ends at ‘your son stole,’ the omitted transition instead has the brothers return and tell their father the report.
rows.anchor: ومن يرى أن كلام كبيرهم تم في قوله: إن ابنك سرق، فإنه يجعل الكلام هنالك تقديره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s words express suspicion of his sons, as in the earlier Joseph episode; his suspicion proved true then but was not verified in this episode.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: بل سولت لكم أنفسكم أمرا. إنما هو ظن سيء بهم، كما كان في قصة يوسف قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سولت means adorned, deluded, or made something into a desired object; السول is what a person longs for and pursues.
rows.anchor: وسولت معناه: زينت وخيلت وجعلته سولا، والسول ما يتمناه الإنسان ويحرص عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Beautiful patience’ can be a nominal subject with an omitted predicate such as better or most fitting, or a predicate of an omitted ‘my affair’ or ‘my patience’; the latter better suits an indefinite predicate.
rows.anchor: وإما خبر ابتداء تقديره، فأمري أو شأني، أو صبري صبر جميل وهذا أليق بالنكرة أن تكون خبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beautiful patience means neither complaining to people nor becoming impatient with God’s decree.
rows.anchor: ومعنى وصفه بالجمال: أنه ليس فيه شكوى إلى بشر ولا ضجر بقضاء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob hopes God will reunite him with Joseph, Benjamin, and Reuben, who remained behind; he bases hope on Joseph’s dream, trust in God, and the Egyptian king’s promise to pray for a reunion before death.
rows.anchor: ثم ترجى عليه السلام من الله أن يجبرهم عليه وهم يوسف وبنيامين وروبيل الذي لم يبرح الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God All-knowing and Wise suits Jacob’s hope of seeing his sons and submits to divine wisdom in everything that happened.
rows.anchor: والوصف «بالعلم والإحكام» لائق بما يرجوه من لقاء بنيه، وفيها تسليم لحكمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob turns away because he distrusts and suspects his sons’ account, then grieves and laments.
rows.anchor: المعنى: أنه لما ساء ظنه بهم ولم يصدق قولهم بل استراب به، تولى عنهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says this community was specially given the formula of returning to God, pointing to Jacob’s cry of grief.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: خصت هذه الأمة بالاسترجاع ألا ترى إلى قول يعقوب: يا أسفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: يا أسفى means ‘O my grief’; the possessive ya is replaced by alif, as in other vocatives, and grief is addressed as if summoned to come at its appointed moment.
rows.anchor: والمراد: «يا أسفي» . لكن هذه لغة من يرد ياء الإضافة ألفا نحو: يا غلاما ويا أبتا

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One view takes the phrase as a lament, with omission of the emphatic lamentation hāʾ to show Jacob’s effort to endure within his commitment to patience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قوله: يا أسفى على جهة الندبة، وحذف الهاء التي هي في الندبة علامة المبالغة في الحزن

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Other interpretations take Jacob’s cry as an appeal for help; the author says returning to God and crying ‘O my grief’ can coexist.
rows.anchor:
وقيل: قوله: يا أسفى نداء فيه استغاثة.
قال القاضي أبو محمد: ولا يبعد أن يجتمع الاسترجاع ويا أسفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s eyes whitened from prolonged weeping, itself the consequence of grief.
rows.anchor: وابيضت عيناه أي من ملازمة البكاء الذي هو ثمرة الحزن

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan transmits from the Prophet that Jacob grieved like seventy bereaved women, received the reward of a hundred martyrs, and never thought ill of God.
rows.anchor: وروي «أن يعقوب عليه السلام حزن حزن سبعين ثكلى وأعطي أجر مائة شهيد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read الحزن with both consonants open; Qatada reads both with damma, while the majority reads the first with damma and the second silent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس ومجاهد «من الحزن» بفتح الحاء والزاي، وقرأ قتادة بضمهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: كظيم is most clearly an active participle, one who restrains grief: Jacob complained to no one and kept his distress in his heart rather than releasing it through complaint, anger, or obscenity.
rows.anchor: وجري كظيم على باب كاظم أبين

rows.speaker: ناس
rows.claim: Some interpret كظيم as passive مكظوم, as in Jonah’s description, meaning filled and constricted by grief; others gloss it as distressed or worn down, all near in meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال ناس: كظيم بمعني: مكظوم

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: Munthir ibn Sa'id distinguishes asaf: when caused by someone inferior it means anger, but when caused by what one cannot withstand it means grief and sorrow.
rows.anchor: وقال منذر بن سعيد: الأسف إذا كان من جهة من هو أقل من الإنسان فهو غضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author clarifies that asaf is used for both anger and grief, with context determining which condition it denotes.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وتحرير هذا المنزع: أن الأسف يقال في الغضب ويقال في الحزن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After an oath, لا is omitted from تفتؤ because the context makes the negation clear; poetry provides parallels.
rows.anchor: المعنى تالله لا تفتأ فتحذف لا في هذه الموضع من القسم لدلالة الكلام عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qays’s line ‘I will remain seated’ means ‘I will not cease sitting,’ illustrating omitted لا after an oath.
rows.anchor: فقلت يمين الله أبرح قاعدا ... ولو قطعوا رأسي لديك وأوصالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another poet’s statement that a high mountain figure will remain means ‘will not remain,’ again supplying omitted negation after an oath.
rows.anchor: تالله يبقى على الأيام ذو حيد ... بمشمخر به الظيان والآس

rows.speaker: الزجاجي
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaji says ما too can be omitted in this construction, but some grammarians call that mistaken; the author argues the relevant omission is لا, not ما.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاجي: وقد تحذف أيضا ما في هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the claim that ما is omitted: a cited line’s clause about the fire drill requires omitted لا; فتىء works like زال and برح in meaning and syntax.
rows.anchor: وفتىء بمنزلة زال وبرح في المعنى والعمل، تقول: والله لا فتئت قاعدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A line by Aws ibn Hajar uses فتئت with the sense ‘I did not cease,’ supporting the verb’s usage.
rows.anchor:
ومنه قول أوس بن حجر: [الطويل]
فما فتئت حتى كأن غبارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: حرض means one weakened by age, love, or grief until body, organs, and senses deteriorate; the common reading has fatḥa on both consonants.
rows.anchor: «الحرض» : الذي قد نهكه الهرم أو الحب أو الحزن

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads حرض with both consonants carrying damma; another group has damma on ح and sukūn on ر. The noun functions as an invariant verbal noun adjective.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن بن أبي الحسن بضمهما، وقرأت فرقة «حرضا» بضم الحاء وسكون الراء

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: For al-Hasan’s reading, one explanation is that حرض means the decayed remnants of tooth-cleaning material.
rows.anchor: وقيل في قراءة الحسن: انه يراد: فتات الأشنان أي باليا متعتتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic uses حارض for a person worn down by worry or age; a cited al-A'sha line witnesses the word, and امرؤ القيس attests محرض.
rows.anchor: ويقال من هذا المعنى الذي هو شن الهم والهرم: رجل حارض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: حرض generally means ruined and near death; Mujahid says below death, while Qatada, al-Dahhak, and al-Hasan say worn out and old, and Ibn Ishaq says corrupt and irrational.
rows.anchor:
قال مجاهد: «الحرض» : ما دون الموت، قال قتادة:
«الحرض» : البالي الهرم، وقال نحوه الضحاك والحسن

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq glosses حرض as corrupted and without reason: the sons reproach Jacob for remembering Joseph until near death or death itself.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: حرضا معناه فاسد لا عقل له فكأنهم قالوا على جهة التعنيف له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob answers that he is not panicking or impatient in a way deserving reproach; he complains to God, which is no cause for blame.
rows.anchor: فأجابهم يعقوب عليه السلام رادا عليهم: أي أني لست ممن يجزع ويضجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: بث is what a person has resolved to reveal from the heart; it most often refers to painful matters, though it can mean something hidden generally.
rows.anchor: و «البث» ما في صدر الإنسان مما هو معتزم أن يبثه وينشره

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda and others define بث as the most intense grief; examples include the Umm Zar' report and the expression ‘I disclose my story to you.’
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة وغيره: «البث» : أشد الحزن، وقد يستعمل «البث» في المخفي على الجملة

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: Isa reads وحزني with fatḥa on both ح and ز.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى: «وحزني» بفتح الحاء والزاي

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: A report says an aged Jacob entered Pharaoh’s court, who mistook him for Abraham; Jacob attributed his condition to long time and many sorrows, and God reproached him for complaining to creatures, after which he sought forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري بسند: أن يعقوب دخل على فرعون وقد سقط حاجباه على عينيه من الكبر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reports that eighty years passed from Joseph’s departure until Jacob came to him; grief never left Jacob, he wept until blind, and no one then was more honored by God.
rows.anchor:
وأسند الطبري إلى الحسن قال: كان بين خروج يوسف عن يعقوب إلى دخول يعقوب على يوسف ثمانون
سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s knowledge from God may mean his good opinion of God’s customary care, the awaited dream, or his impression from Egypt’s king promising to pray for a reunion; the last is the previously mentioned good opinion.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أنه أشار إلى حسن ظنه بالله وجميل عادة الله عنده، ويحتمل أنه أشار إلى الرؤيا المنتظرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob sends his sons back to the land they came from, where they left Benjamin and Reuben, to search carefully for Joseph and Benjamin.
rows.anchor: المعنى: اذهبوا إلى الأرض التي جئتم منها وتركتم أخويكم بنيامين وروبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تحسس is searching with the senses, especially sight and hearing; it can be used for good, as here, or evil, as in the prohibition against spying.
rows.anchor: والتحسس: طلب الشيء بالحواس من البصر والسمع، ويستعمل في الخير والشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase من يوسف depends on an omitted object: seek news or the reality of Joseph’s situation, omitted for concision because the wording makes it clear.
rows.anchor: وقوله: من يوسف يتعلق بمحذوف يعمل فيه تحسسوا التقدير: فتحسسوا نبأ أو حقيقة من أمر يوسف

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some read تيأسوا, while another group reads تأيسوا; al-A'raj reads تئسوا with kasra on the initial tāʾ.
rows.anchor: رأت فرقة: «تيأسوا» وقرأت فرقة «تأيسوا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph and Benjamin are singled out because Reuben remained by choice, while these two were prevented from returning.
rows.anchor: وخص يوسف وبنيامين بالذكر لأن روبيل إنما بقي مختارا. وهذان قد منعا الأوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: روح here means mercy and relief; despair of God’s mercy is assigned to disbelievers because it entails denying lordship or ignorance of God’s attributes.
rows.anchor: و «الروح» : الرحمة. ثم جعل اليأس من رحمة الله وتفريجه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, Qatada, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read روح with ḍamma on ر, glossing it as the life-spirit God gave: one whose spirit remains is still hoped for.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وقتادة وعمر بن عبد العزيز «من روح الله» بضم الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two cited poems support hoping for the living or absent person: one says hope remains for those not buried, and Ubayd says an absent person returns whereas the dead do not.
rows.anchor: وكل ذي غيبة يؤوب ... وغائب الموت لا يؤوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report of a man who ordered his burned, scattered remains to avoid God’s punishment does not entail unbelief: the Prophet’s report that God forgave him means he died a believer.
rows.anchor: لأن قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في آخر الحديث فغفر الله له يقتضي أنه مات مؤمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report can be read as qadara meaning constricted and carefully reckoned, or as ability: he wrongly thought resurrection after scattering impossible, but this mistaken view does not make him an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: إما على أن قدر بمعنى ضيق وناقش الحساب، فذلك معنى بين

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash reports Ibn Masud’s reading من فضل and Ubayy ibn Ka'b’s reading من رحمة الله.
rows.anchor: قال النقاش: وقرأ ابن مسعود «من فضل» وقرأ أبي بن كعب: «من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account omits the brothers’ journey from Syria to Egypt and their arrival; the pronoun in عليه refers to Joseph.
rows.anchor: أنهم نفذوا من الشام إلى مصر ووصلوها والضمير في عليه عائد على يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their الضر refers both to famine and to the affair of their brother, which distressed their father and all of them.
rows.anchor: والضر أرادوا به المسغبة التي كانوا بسبيلها وأمر أخيهم الذي أهم أباهم وغم جميعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: بضاعة is a portion of capital for buying something; in juristic custom it is money whose carrier has no share in the profit.
rows.anchor: و «البضاعة» : القطعة من المال يقصد بها شراء شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مزجاة means pushed or passed along with difficulty; the root describes gently driving clouds or camels, as several poets’ lines illustrate.
rows.anchor: وال مزجاة معناها المدفوعة المتحيل لها، ومنه إزجاء السحاب، ومنه إزجاء الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that something tenderly ushered along is مزجى; low-value coins need apology and intercession, so the brothers called their payment مزجاة.
rows.anchor: فجملة هذا أن من يسوق شيئا ويتلطف في تسييره فقد أزجاه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says their money consisted of debased coins; al-Hasan says it was a small amount, and Ibn Jubayr says it was deficient.
rows.anchor: فقيل: كان ذلك لأنها كانت زيوفا- قاله ابن عباس- وقال الحسن: كانت قليلة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الحارث
rows.claim: Views that the goods were trade merchandise include ghee and wool according to Abdullah ibn al-Harith, dried wild game according to Ali, and pine nuts with green grain according to Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam.
rows.anchor: فقيل: كانت السمن والصوف- قاله عبد الله بن الحارث- وقال علي بن أبي طالب: كانت قديد وحش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed goods are pistachios, called green grain by the author, plus mash, cotton, ropes, packs, and saddles.
rows.anchor:
وقال أبو صالح وزيد بن أسلم: كانت الصنوبر والحبة الخضراء.
قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهي الفستق

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Makkī quotes Malik as defining مزجاة as a prize or gift; the author finds no basis for this and says the meaning contradicts the verse, perhaps due to a miscopied word.
rows.anchor:
وحكى مكي أن مالكا رحمه الله قال: المزجاة: الجائزة.
قال القاضي أبو محمد: ولا أعرف لهذا وجها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Malik relied on this verse to argue that measuring grain is the seller’s duty; the verse supports this plainly but does not state it definitively.
rows.anchor: واستند مالك رحمه الله في أن الكيل على البائع إلى هذه الآية، وذلك ظاهر منها وليس بنص

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and others say ‘be charitable to us’ asks Joseph to make up the difference between sound coins and their low-grade payment.
rows.anchor: وقولهم: وتصدق علينا معناه بما بين الدراهم الجياد وهذه المزجاة، قاله السدي وغيره

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn Uyayna says charity was lawful for earlier prophets and forbidden only to Muhammad; the author rejects this by citing the prophetic statement that charity is unlawful for prophets.
rows.anchor:
قاله سفيان بن عيينة.
قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا ضعيف، يرده حديث النبي

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group says charity was forbidden to them, but they used the phrase as a conciliatory bargaining expression, like asking a seller to reduce a price without literally seeking a gift.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: كانت الصدقة عليهم محرمة ولكن قالوا هذا تجوزا واستعطافا منهم في المبايعة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the requested charity was returning Benjamin to his father, while the brothers still requested a full measure in the sale.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: إنما خصوا بقولهم وتصدق علينا أمر أخيهم بنيامين

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash calls ‘God rewards the charitable’ an allusive escape from lying: believing Joseph an unbeliever, they avoided explicitly promising him an afterlife reward while leaving room to reinterpret their words.
rows.anchor: قال النقاش: يقال: هو من المعاريض التي هي مندوحة عن الكذب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Judah was the bearer of good news because he had brought the bloodied shirt earlier.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس: أن البشير كان يهوذا لأنه كان جاء بقميص الدم

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل بن الجوهري
rows.claim: A preacher quoted by the author’s father says Judah volunteered to carry the joyful shirt because he had previously carried the shirt of grief; al-Suddi reports the same account.
rows.anchor: قال يهوذا لإخوته: قد علمتم أني ذهبت إليه بقميص الترحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ارتد means ‘returned’ and can be intransitive or causative; بصيرا means seeing.
rows.anchor: وارتد معناه: رجع هو، يقال: ارتد الرجل ورده غيره، وبصيرا معناه: مبصرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s reminder that he knew from God likely refers to his waiting for the dream’s fulfillment, though it may refer simply to his good opinion of God.
rows.anchor: وهذا- والله أعلم- هو انتظاره لتأويل الرؤيا- ويحتمل أن يشير إلى حسن ظنه بالله تعالى فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob asked the bearer what religion Joseph followed; hearing that he was Muslim, Jacob said the blessing was now complete.
rows.anchor: وروي: أنه قال للبشير: على أي دين تركت يوسف؟ قال: على الإسلام قال: الحمد لله، الآن كملت النعمة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The Ibn Masud codex adds من بين يدي العير after ‘when the bearer came.’
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف ابن مسعود: «فلما أن جاء البشير من بين يدي العير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians cited by al-Tabari call أن after لما or حتى an extra particle, since Arabic permits both forms.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن بعض النحويين أنه قال: أن في قوله: فلما أن جاء البشير زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the brothers sought Jacob’s prayer after Joseph had forgiven them because they realized that his pardon and Jacob’s pardon would not help unless God forgave them; they acknowledged their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: روي أن يوسف عليه السلام لما غفر لإخوته، وتحققوا أيضا أن يعقوب يغفر لهم

rows.speaker: محارب بن دثار
rows.claim: A report from Muharib ibn Dithar says Abdullah ibn Masud explained Jacob’s delay as waiting until dawn; the author supports this with the hadith about God answering prayer and forgiveness in the last third of each night.
rows.anchor: وروي عن محارب بن دثار أنه قال: كان عم لي يأتي المسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dawn interpretation is strengthened by the verse praising those who seek forgiveness before dawn.
rows.anchor: ويقويه قوله تعالى: والمستغفرين بالأسحار

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says Jacob delayed his sons until the night prayer.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: إنما سوفهم يعقوب إلى قيام الليل

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says Jacob delayed them until the white nights, when supplication is answered.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة- منهم سعيد بن جبير- سوفهم يعقوب إلى الليالي البيض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Other views place the delay on Friday night; Ibn Abbas attributes to the Prophet a report that Jacob waited until Friday arrived.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن عباس هذا التأويل عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، قال: «أخرهم يعقوب حتى تأتي له الجمعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob reassures his sons by affirming that God is the Forgiving and Merciful.
rows.anchor: ثم رجاهم يعقوب عليه السلام بقوله: إنه هو الغفور الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text omits Jacob gathering his household, traveling, and reaching Joseph before their entrance.
rows.anchor: هاهنا محذوفات يدل عليها الظاهر، وهي: فرحل يعقوب بأهله أجمعين وساروا حتى بلغوا يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: آوى means he gathered them close and displayed protection; a prophetic hadith uses the same verb for one of three men sheltered by God.
rows.anchor: وآوى معناه: ضم وأظهر الحماية بهما، وفي الحديث: «أما أحدهم فأوى إلى الله فآواه الله

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq and al-Hasan identify the two parents as Jacob and Joseph’s mother; the author finds this most apparent unless a reliable chain establishes that she had died.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد «بالأبوين» : أباه وأمه- قاله ابن إسحاق والحسن

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawi reports that the two parents were Jacob and Joseph’s maternal grandmother.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أباه وجدته- أم أمه- حكاه الزهراوي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the mother had died, so the two parents mean Jacob and Joseph’s maternal aunt.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أباه وخالته، لأن أمه قد كانت ماتت- قاله السدي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The Ibn Masud codex adds ‘and his brothers’ after saying Joseph received his parents.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف ابن مسعود: «آوى إليه أبويه وإخوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Enter Egypt’ means settle and reside there, since they had already entered; al-Suddi alternatively says Joseph spoke while meeting them on the road.
rows.anchor: وقوله: ادخلوا مصر معناه: تمكنوا واسكنوا واستقروا، لأنهم قد كانوا دخلوا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception إن شاء الله is a Qur'anic model for mentioning God’s will in future plans; Ibn Jurayj connects it semantically to Jacob’s promise to seek forgiveness, but the author finds that weak.
rows.anchor: وهذا الاستثناء هو الذي ندب القرآن إليه، أن يقوله الإنسان في جميع ما ينفذه بقوله في المستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: العرش is the royal throne; خروا means they fell toward the ground.
rows.anchor: والعرش: سرير الملك، وكل ما عرش فهو عريش وعرش

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Prostration was either the familiar face-to-ground act or a deep bow-like royal greeting; all exegetes agree it was greeting, not worship. Qatada says it was the customary greeting for kings; Hasan takes the pronoun as referring to God.
rows.anchor: وأجمع المفسرون أن ذلك السجود- على أي هيئة كان- فإنما كان تحية لا عبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Hasan’s claim that the prostration pronoun refers to God.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: ورد على هذا القول

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari relates that Jacob arrived leaning on Judah, asked whether the approaching ruler was Pharaoh, and learned it was Joseph; Jacob prevented Joseph from greeting first, and Joseph saluted him as remover of sorrows.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري: أن يعقوب لما بلغ مصر في جملته كلم يوسف فرعون في تلقيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another story says Joseph asked Jacob to enter Pharaoh’s court gratefully; Pharaoh questioned his aging, and a revelation rebuked Jacob for complaining to someone unable to harm or benefit him, after which he sought forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا الوقت قال يوسف ليعقوب: إن فرعون قد أحسن إلينا فادخل عليه شاكرا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الشيباني
rows.claim: Abu Amr al-Shaybani reports that Gabriel reprimanded Joseph for walking ahead of his father and warned that no prophet would descend from his line.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو الشيباني: تقدم يوسف يعقوب في المشي في بعض تلك المواطن فهبط جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says the family’s prostration is the fulfillment of his earlier dream of eleven stars, the sun, and the moon.
rows.anchor: المعنى: قال يوسف ليعقوب: هذا السجود الذي كان منكم، هو ما آلت إليه رؤياي قديما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘My Lord made it true’ begins Joseph’s enumeration of God’s favors.
rows.anchor: وقوله: قد جعلها ربي حقا ابتداء تعديد نعم الله تعالى عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أحسن بي means God brought and attached His kindness to Joseph; compared with أحسن إلي or أحسن في, bi best suits Joseph receiving a good he had not sought as an end.
rows.anchor: أي أوقع وناط إحسانه بي. فهذا منحى في وصول الإحسان بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Ubayy’s expression أحسن في موالي illustrates a distinct construction for kindness.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول عبد الله بن أبي ابن سلول: يا محمد أحسن في موالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph mentions release from prison but omits release from the pit to avoid renewing his brothers’ shame and stirring their resentment.
rows.anchor: وذكر يوسف عليه السلام إخراجه من السجن، وترك إخراجه من الجب لوجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reason Joseph mentions prison rather than the pit is that the pit led to slavery, whereas prison led to kingship, making the favor clearer.
rows.anchor: والوجه الآخر: أنه خرج من الجب إلى الرق، ومن السجن إلى الملك فالنعمة هنا أوضح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coming from the desert gathers the family and marks movement from hardship to settled prosperity; Jacob lived in rural Palestine on Syria’s edge as a herdsman.
rows.anchor: وقوله: وجاء بكم من البدو يعم جمع الشمل والتنقل من الشقاوة إلى النعمة بسكنى الحاضرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: نزغ means acting to corrupt and disrupt; a prophetic saying warns against a weapon being offered to a brother lest Satan cause harm.
rows.anchor: ونزغ معناه: فعل فعلا أفسد به، ومنه قول النبي عليه السلام:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph mentions his brothers’ wrongdoing to show how favor is especially welcome after hardship and affliction.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذكر يوسف هذا القدر من أمر إخوته ليبين حسن موقع النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لما يشاء means whatever matters God wills to do.
rows.anchor: وقوله: لما يشاء أي من الأمور أن يفعله

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: Reports differ on the interval between Joseph’s dream and fulfillment: Salman al-Farisi and Abdullah ibn Shaddad say forty years; Ibn Shaddad calls it the longest-delayed dream.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة أربعون سنة- هذا قول سلمان الفارسي وعبد الله بن شداد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan, Jasr ibn Farqad, and Fudayl ibn Iyad say eighty years; other reported estimates are eighteen (Ibn Ishaq), twenty-two (al-Naqqash), thirty, thirty-five (Qatada), and thirty-six (al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr).
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة- منهم الحسن وجسر بن فرقد وفضيل بن عياض- ثمانون سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Joseph lived to 120 and Jacob stayed with him more than twenty years before dying.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن يوسف عليه السلام عمر مائة وعشرين سنة. وقيل: إن يعقوب بقي عند يوسف نيفا على عشرين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says only divine revelation explains why Joseph did not tell his father after leaving prison and attaining status: God intended to test Jacob and his sons and bring them together in that manner.
rows.anchor:
ولا وجه في ترك تعريف يوسف أباه بحاله منذ خرج من السجن إلى العز إلا
الوحي من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says the revelation came in the pit, citing the promise in 12:15; the author calls this possible.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: كان ذلك الوحي في الجب، وهو قوله تعالى: وأوحينا إليه لتنبئنهم بأمرهم هذا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan reports that when the bearer arrived Jacob had nothing to reward him with and had not baked bread for seven nights; he prayed that God ease the bearer’s death throes.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: إنه لما ورده البشير لم يجد عنده شيئا يثيبه به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob complained that God had blinded him and hidden Joseph; God promised their return but explained the trial by an unsatisfied poor neighbor smelling lamb cooked at Jacob’s home, after which Jacob invited the neighbor to meals.
rows.anchor: أنه لما اشتد بلاؤه وقال: يا رب أعميت بصري وغيبت عني يوسف، أفما ترحمني

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari relates that the sons asked Jacob to seek their forgiveness; Jacob prayed with Joseph and the brothers behind him for twenty years until revelation said they were forgiven and granted prophetic covenants after him.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري: أنه لما اجتمع شمله كلفه بنوه أن يدعو الله لهم حتى يأتي الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob asked Joseph to bury him in Syria; after Jacob died Joseph’s body was carried there, while Moses later carried Joseph’s bones from Egypt to be buried with the ancestors.
rows.anchor: ومن أخباره: أنه لما حضرته الوفاة أوصى إلى يوسف أن يدفنه بالشام

none: Bare section heading only; no commentary claim follows in this segment.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reads آتيتن and علمتن without the final yāʾ as a lighter form; Ibn Dharr reads the opening without قد.
rows.anchor: بحذف الياء على التخفيف، وقرأ ابن ذر «رب آتيتني» بغير «قد»

rows.speaker: مفسرون
rows.claim: Many commentators say Joseph counted God’s favors, longed to meet God and the righteous among his forebears and other believers, and therefore wished for death and reunion; Ibn Abbas says no prophet but Joseph wished for death.
rows.anchor: وذكر كثير من المفسرين: أن يوسف عليه السلام لما عدد في هذه الآية نعم الله عنده تشوق إلى لقاء ربه

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi’s interpretation, which the author calls stronger, denies that Joseph wishes for death: he asks to die when his term arrives as a Muslim and to join the righteous.
rows.anchor: وذكر المهدوي تأويلا آخر- وهو الأقوى عندي- أن ليس في الآية تمني موت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author distinguishes wishing to meet God from wishing for death; Joseph asks only that his eventual end come in Islam, consistent with the prohibition on wishing for death because of worldly harm.
rows.anchor: وإنما تمنى الموافاة على الإسلام لا الموت. وورد عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «لا يتمنين أحدكم الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic supplication asks God to take the speaker if He brings a trial among people, provided he is not tried; Umar likewise asks for death without falling short or becoming incapable.
rows.anchor: وإذا أردت في الناس فتنة فاقبضني إليك غير مفتون» ، وروي عن عمر بن الخطاب أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads the prohibition on wishing for death as concerning worldly harms such as poverty or illness; wishing for death to avoid religious corruption remains permissible.
rows.anchor:
فيشبه أن قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: لضر نزل به- إنما يريد ضرر
الدنيا كالفقر والمرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith about someone wishing to be in another man’s grave because of trials, not religion, implies that a religious motive for such a wish is allowed.
rows.anchor: يأتي على الناس زمان يمر فيه الرجل بقبر الرجل فيقول: يا ليتني مكانه، ليس به الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: من الملك and من تأويل الأحاديث may use من partitivally or to explain the kind; أحاديث means dreams or stories of prophets and peoples.
rows.anchor: قيل: من للتبعيض وقيل: لبيان الجنس وكذلك في قوله: من تأويل الأحاديث والمراد بقوله: الأحاديث الأحلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فاطر is vocative; ولي means the one who manages Joseph’s affairs and guarantees his support and mercy.
rows.anchor: وقوله: فاطر منادى، وقوله: أنت وليي أي القائم بأمري الكفيل بنصرتي ورحمتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘That’ points to the story of Joseph and indirectly challenges Quraysh, presenting a sign of Muhammad’s truth and a critique of those who deny him.
rows.anchor: ذلك إشارة إلى ما تقدم من قصة يوسف، وهذه الآية تعريض لقريش وتنبيه على آية صدق محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns refer to Joseph’s brothers; أجمعوا means they resolved firmly, the matter was throwing Joseph into the well, and plotting is arranging harm while deception induces someone to act to his own detriment.
rows.anchor:
والضمير في لديهم عائد إلى إخوة يوسف، وكذلك الضمائر إلى آخر الآية، وأجمعوا معناه:
عزموا وجزموا

rows.speaker: أبو عمران الجوني
rows.claim: Abu Imran al-Jawni says God did not tell the story to shame Joseph’s brothers, who are prophets among the people of Paradise, but to prevent His servants from despairing.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن أبي عمران الجوني أنه قال: والله ما قص الله نبأهم ليعيرهم بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding account of unseen events is evidence of Muhammad’s prophethood, yet most people will not believe despite his earnest wish; only those God wills believe. The phrase ولو حرصت is an eloquent parenthesis.
rows.anchor: هاتان الآيتان تدلان أن الآية التي قبلهما فيها تعريض لقريش ومعاصري محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that Muhammad asks no payment rebukes unbelievers and proves his case: no one can claim that he preaches for money.
rows.anchor: وقوله: وما تسئلهم الآية، توبيخ للكفرة وإقامة الحجة عليهم

rows.speaker: مبشر بن عبيد
rows.claim: Mubashir ibn Ubayd reads نسألهم with first-person plural nun rather than تسألهم.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مبشر بن عبيد: «وما نسألهم» بالنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is then described as a reminder and admonition for all peoples.
rows.anchor: ثم ابتدأ الله تعالى الإخبار عن كتابه العزيز أنه ذكر وموعظة لجميع العالم

rows.speaker: الجماعة
rows.claim: Most read وكأين with hamza and doubled y; Ibn Kathir reads وكائن with a long alif and hamza, from the active participle of كان, but both mean ‘how many.’ Sibawayh parses the common form as kāf joined to أي.
rows.anchor: وقرأت الجماعة «وكأين» بهمز الألف وشد الياء، قال سيبويه: هي كاف التشبيه اتصلت بأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are creatures and events set up for reflection, pointing to God; when unbelievers perceive them they fail to reflect because desire and heedlessness make them act like people turning away.
rows.anchor: آية هنا المخلوقات المنصوبة للاعتبار والحوادث الدالة على الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line about the morning breeze passing the residents of a valley while its gust breaks the speaker’s heart illustrates passing by without response.
rows.anchor: تمر الصبا صفحا بساكن ذي الغضا ... ويصدع قلبي أن يهب هبوبها

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi reads والأرض in the accusative with an omitted verb and pauses after السماوات; Ikrima and Amr ibn Fa'id read it nominatively as a new subject, with يمرون as predicate; in the genitive reading, يمرون modifies آية.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السدي «والأرض» بالنصب بإضمار فعل، والوقف- على هذا- في السماوات

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The Abdullah codex reads ‘and the earth, they walk upon it.’
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف عبد الله: «والأرض يمشون عليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas applies the verse to People of the Book who affirm God but associate partners by rejecting His prophet or calling Ezra and Christ sons of God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هي في أهل الكتاب الذين يؤمنون بالله ثم يشركون من حيث كفروا بنبيه

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima, Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd apply it to Arab polytheists: their acknowledgment of God as creator, provider, and giver of life is linguistic faith followed by idol worship.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة ومجاهد وقتادة وابن زيد هي في كفار العرب، وإيمانهم هو إقرارهم بالخالق والرازق

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One view says the verse arose from Quraysh’s circumambulation chant, which acknowledged one God while making an exception for a partner owned by Him; the Prophet told them to stop before that addition.
rows.anchor:
وقيل: هذه الآية نزلت بسبب قول قريش في الطواف والتلبية:
لبيك لا شريك لك إلا شريك هو لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: غاشية is something that covers, veils, or darkens; Mubashir reads يأتيهم with yāʾ, and sudden arrival is especially difficult.
rows.anchor: غاشية ما يغشي ويغطي ويغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the immediate context addresses unbelievers, sinners can take warning: their faith may be real while their shirk is figurative, like showing off, which the Prophet called minor shirk.
rows.anchor: فإن العصاة يأخذون من ألفاظها بحظ، ويكون الإيمان حقيقة والشرك لغويا كالرياء

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: ‘This is my path’ refers to the whole invitation to Islam and its law; Ibn Zayd glosses it as the Prophet’s affair, practice, and way.
rows.anchor:
إشارة إلى دعوة الإسلام والشريعة بأسرها. قال ابن زيد:
المعنى: هذا أمري وسنتي ومنهاجي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reads هذا سبيلي rather than the feminine هذه سبيلي.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود: «قل هذا سبيلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سبيل and طريق, both meaning path, may be masculine or feminine; بصيرة means a person’s conviction in truth and certainty, and can also mean a blood mark on a spearhead in a hadith.
rows.anchor: والسبيل» : المسلك، وتؤنث وتذكر، وكذلك الطريق، وبصيرة: اسم لمعتقد الإنسان في الأمر من الحق واليقين

rows.speaker: الأشعر الجعفي
rows.claim: Al-Ash'ar al-Ju'fi’s poem uses بصائر for the marks of a murdered ally’s blood on the shoulders of those who sold him.
rows.anchor: راحوا بصائرهم على أكتافهم ... وبصيرتي يعدو بها عتد وأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author alternatively reads بصيرة in the poem as true conviction: the group put its belief in seeking Hell behind its back, as in a familiar expression.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون «البصيرة» في بيت الأشعر على المعتقد الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أنا ومن اتبعني may coordinate with the hidden subject of أدعو, meaning the Prophet and his followers invite; alternatively the entire verse commands right and calls unbelievers and sinners to God.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون تأكيدا للضمير في أدعوا ويحتمل أن تكون الآية كلها أمارة بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سبحان الله means declaring God transcendent; the Prophet is told to say this and disavow associationism.
rows.anchor: وسبحان الله تنزيه لله، أي وقل: سبحان الله، وقل متبرئا من الشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the passage from ‘This is my path’ to the end was inscribed on Joseph’s banners.
rows.anchor: وروي أن هذه الآية: قل هذه سبيلي إلى آخرها كانت مرقومة على رايات يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers people who find human messengers strange or demand that a messenger be an angel or king.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تتضمن الرد على مستغربي إرسال الرسل من البشر كالطائفة التي قالت: أبعث الله بشرا رسولا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read يوحى with yāʾ and fatḥa on ح; Hafs reads نوحي with nūn and kasra, as do Abu Abd al-Rahman and Talha.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «يوحى إليهم» بالياء وفتح الحاء، وهي قراءة عاصم في رواية أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: القرى means cities; the verse singles them out rather than nomadic tent-dwellers, whom the author characterizes as especially rough and ignorant. Ibn Zayd says town-dwellers are more knowledgeable and forbearing.
rows.anchor: والقرى: المدن، وخصصها دون القوم المنتوين- أهل العمود- فإنهم في كل أمة أهل جفاء وجهالة مفرطة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says God never sent a messenger from among nomadic people, women, or jinn.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: لم يبعث الله رسولا قط من أهل البادية ولا من النساء ولا من الجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says nomadic withdrawal is disliked except during persecution or when fleeing to preserve religion, citing prophetic reports about keeping sheep, Salama’s permission, and disapproval of becoming a Bedouin.
rows.anchor: والتبدي مكروه إلا في الفتن وحين يفر بالدين

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Muadh compares Satan to a wolf that takes isolated sheep, urging people away from ravines and toward mosques, congregations, and the community.
rows.anchor: الشيطان ذيب الإنسان كذيب الغنم يأخذ الشاة القاصية فإياكم والشعاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s residence in the desert does not contradict the claim: it was a settled place with homes, and it was called desert relative to Egypt’s cities.
rows.anchor: ويعترض هذا ببدو يعقوب، وينفصل عن ذلك بوجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The audience is directed to consider the fate of earlier peoples who rejected messengers and were overtaken by punishment, then urged to prepare for the afterlife and avoid ruinous sins.
rows.anchor: ثم أحالهم على الاعتبار في الأمم السالفة في أقطار الأرض التي كذبت رسلها فحاق بها عذاب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife home adds to God’s favor: He punished unbelievers and saved believers, so the afterlife is better for believers.
rows.anchor: وقوله: ولدار الآخرة زيادة في وصف إنعامه على المؤمنين، أي عذب الكفار ونجى المؤمنين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra treats دار الآخرة as adding a thing to itself, like مسجد الجامع or the cited poetic ديار عبس; Basran grammarians posit an omitted noun such as life or period.
rows.anchor: فقال الفراء: هي إضافة الشيء إلى نفسه كما قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that generic nouns need a qualifier to specify their intended sense; they may be linked to another genus, a quality, or a proper name.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأسماء التي هي للأجناس كمسجد وثوب وحق وجبل ونحو ذلك- إذا نطق بها الناطق لم يدر ما يريد بها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and several readers read يعقلون with yāʾ; Abu Hatim says the common reading uses second-person tāʾ, and transmission differs for al-A'mash.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعمش والأعرج وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وعلقمة «يعقلون» بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding verse implies that messengers from the towns preached, were rejected, and their people punished; that context makes حتى appropriate as the story turns to the messengers’ loss of hope.
rows.anchor: ويتضمن قوله تعالى: أفلم يسيروا في الأرض فينظروا كيف كان عاقبة الذين من قبلهم

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir and others read كُذِّبوا with ḍamma on ك and a doubled ذ; the author begins explaining it as the messengers becoming certain that their peoples had rejected them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والحسن وعائشة- بخلاف

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: The other reading has ḍamma on ك and an undoubled ذ; it is transmitted from Ali and many others, including Ubayy, Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-A'mash.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون «كذبوا» بضم الكاف وكسر الذال وتخفيفها- وهي قراءة علي بن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the doubled reading, الظن may mean certainty with both pronouns referring to the messengers, who knew the idolaters had rejected them; alternatively, الظن keeps its usual sense and refers to the messengers’ fear that early believers had rejected them after delays.
rows.anchor: وأما القراءة الثانية- وهي ضم الكاف وكسر الذال وتخفيفها- فيحتمل أن يكون المعنى- حتى إذا استيأس الرسل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: For the light reading, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr say messengers despaired of their people responding, while the people thought the messengers had lied after respite lasted; then help came.
rows.anchor: هذا مشهور قول ابن عباس وابن جبير

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: In a report, Muslim ibn Yasar says the verse troubled him; Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains that messengers lost hope of response and their people thought them liars, then victory came, prompting Muslim to embrace him gratefully.
rows.anchor: وأسند الطبري: أن مسلم بن يسار قال لسعيد بن جبير: يا أبا عبد الله، آية بلغت مني كل مبلغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author praises the two scholars’ intellectual character in resolving the difficulty.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: فرضي الله عنهم كيف كان خلقهم في العلم

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi prefers the interpretation that the messengers’ audiences thought they had lied; the pronouns can refer to audiences because mentioning messengers entails mention of those sent to.
rows.anchor: ورجح أبو علي الفارسي هذا التأويل، وقال: إن رد الضمير في ظنوا وفي «كذبوا» على المرسل إليهم- وإن كان

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another interpretation of the light reading makes both pronouns refer to the messengers: they weakened and thought God’s informant had lied to them; Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud, and Ibn Jubayr are cited, though they also ask whether messengers were not human.
rows.anchor: وتحتمل هذه القراءة أيضا أن يكون الضمير في ظنوا وفي كذبوا عائد على الرسل

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha and other scholars reject the interpretation that messengers themselves thought they had been lied to; Abu Ali says it is impermissible to attribute this to messengers.
rows.anchor: وردت هذا التأويل عائشة أم المؤمنين وجماعة من أهل العلم، وأعظموا أن توصف الرسل بهذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the correct position is that messengers did not think God’s promise false: such a reading conflicts with their protection and knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا هو الصواب، وأين العصمة والعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the third reading with fatḥa on ك and ذ, the pronouns may refer respectively to audiences and messengers; if both refer to messengers, it returns to the rejected suggestion that they thought themselves conveying a lie.
rows.anchor: وأما القراءة الثالثة- وهي فتح الكاف والذال- فالضمير في ظنوا للمرسل إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s help arrived by punishing unbelieving peoples, saving whichever messengers and followers He chose, and bringing punishment upon criminal unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقوله: جاءهم نصرنا أي بتعذيب أممهم الكافرة، ثم وصف حال مجيء العذاب

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read فننجي with two nūns, from أنجى.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي «فننجي» - بنونين- من أنجى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads فننجي with the second nūn vowelled open, deriving it from نجى ينجي.
rows.anchor:
وقرأ الحسن:
«فننجي» - النون الثانية مفتوحة، وهو من نجى ينجي

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr and Qatada read فنجي with one written nūn and doubled jīm; some explain assimilation, while others say nūn and jīm differ too much in qualities and that the nūn was omitted only in writing, not speech.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو أيضا وقتادة «فنجي» - بنون واحدة وشد الجيم وسكون الياء

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim and Ibn Amir read فنجي with fatḥa on yāʾ on the faʿala pattern.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وابن عامر «فنجي» بفتح الياء على وزن فعل

rows.speaker: هَبِيرَة
rows.claim: A group reads فننجي with two nūns and fatḥa on yāʾ, transmitted by Hubayra from Hafs from Asim; the author calls Hubayra’s reading mistaken.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة «فننجي» - بنونين وفتح الياء- رواها هبيرة عن حفص عن عاصم- وهي غلط من هبيرة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read فنجى as a past verb with light jīm; al-Dani also reports Ibn Muhaysin’s doubled-jīm reading, meaning victory was granted.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن ومجاهد «فنجى» - فعل ماض بتخفيف الجيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: البأس means punishment; Abu Haywa reads يشاء with yāʾ and بأسه with hāʾ, and the verse threatens Muhammad’s contemporary unbelievers.
rows.anchor: و «البأس» : العذاب. وقرأ أبو حيوة «من يشاء» - بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in قصصهم includes Joseph, his parents and brothers, and the other messengers mentioned generally.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قصصهم عام ليوسف وأبويه وإخوته وسائر الرسل الذين ذكروا على الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s story offers lessons in wonders, trials, divine gentleness, and favor, teaching reflective people that every matter comes from God and returns to Him.
rows.anchor: فإذا تأملت قصة يوسف ظهر أن في غرائبها وامتحان الله فيها لقوم في مواضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ما كان حديثا يفترى is a categorical denial; context proves the story is not fabricated through signs of prophethood and inimitability. حديث means a report, not ‘opposite of ancient.’
rows.anchor: وقوله: ما كان صيغة منع، وقرينة الحال تقتضي أن البرهان يقوم على أن ذلك لا يفترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تصديق can be accusative by an implied كان or with لكن understood as لكن; Isa al-Thaqafi reads it and its coordinated words nominatively with an omitted subject ‘it is,’ as Abu Hatim explains; the cited Dhu al-Rumma line admits both, though accusative is better.
rows.anchor: ونصب تصديق إما على إضمار معنى كان، وإما على أن تكون لكن بمعنى لكن المشددة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What was before it’ is the Torah and Gospel, with its pronoun referring to the Qur’an; ‘all things’ means doctrines, rulings, lawful matters, and forbidden matters.
rows.anchor: والذي بين يديه هو التوراة والإنجيل، والضمير في يديه عائد على القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Meccan except for three verses, including 17:73 and 17:76, associated with the visit of Thaqif’s delegation and the Jews’ claim that this was not the land of prophets; 17:80 is also listed.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية إلا ثلاث آيات، قوله عز وجل: وإن كادوا ليفتنونك

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil is cited in connection with the verse about those given knowledge before it.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل وقوله عز وجل إن الذين أوتوا العلم من قبله

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says Isra and Kahf are among the ancient first chapters and part of his early acquired legacy.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود في بني إسرائيل والكهف، إنهن من العتاق الأول وهن من تلادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servant is Muhammad; the author reads أسرى as a transitive causative with an omitted object, ‘the angels carried His servant,’ avoiding literal movement attributed to God, while preserving fluent Arabic.
rows.anchor: لفظ الآية يقتضي أن الله عز وجل أسرى بعبده، وهو محمد عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that movement verbs such as walking, running, and traveling are unsuitable for literal attribution to God; reports such as ‘I came walking’ or ‘running’ must be interpreted to avoid affirming temporal change.
rows.anchor: إذ هو فعل يعطي النقلة كمشى وجرى وأحضر وانتقل، فلا يحسن إسناد شيء من هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively أسرى can mean سارى with an omitted annexed noun, as in God taking away their light.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون أسرى بمعنى سرى على حذف مضاف كنحو قوله تعالى ذهب الله بنورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Isra is reported in all hadith collections and from Companions across Islam, making it mass-transmitted; al-Naqqash counts twenty Companions.
rows.anchor: ووقع الإسراء في جميع مصنفات الحديث، وروي عن الصحابة في كل أقطار الإسلام فهو من المتواتر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most Companions and scholars say the Prophet traveled bodily on Buraq from Mecca to Jerusalem and prayed there.
rows.anchor: وتلقى جل العلماء منهم أن الإسراء كان بشخصه صلى الله عليه وسلم، وأنه ركب البراق من مكة

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa and others say the Prophet did not dismount or enter Jerusalem; Hudhayfa argues that prayer there would have made it obligatory for the community, and says Buraq carried him from Mecca home except during ascent.
rows.anchor: وروى حذيفة وغيره أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لم ينزل عن البراق في بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha and Muawiya say only the Prophet’s soul traveled while his body remained in bed; it was a true vision of divine realities. Hasan and Ibn Ishaq allow this view, with Buraq part of the dream.
rows.anchor:
وقالت عائشة ومعاوية إنما أسري
بنفس رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ولم يفارق شخصه مضجعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The detailed hadith is lengthy in al-Bukhari, Muslim, and other works, so the author abbreviates it here.
rows.anchor: والحديث، قال القاضي أبو محمد، مطول في البخاري ومسلم وغيرهما، فلذلك اختصرنا نصه في هذا الباب

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyab and Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, as cited in al-Tabari, say Buraq was Abraham’s mount for visiting the Sacred House.
rows.anchor: قال ابن المسيب وأبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن في كتاب الطبري: البراق هو دابة إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the majority’s bodily journey: if it had been only a dream, Quraysh’s mockery, Abu Bakr’s distinction for belief, and Umm Hani’s warning not to tell people would make little sense.
rows.anchor: والصحيح ما ذهب إليه الجمهور، ولو كانت منامة ما أمكن قريشا التشنيع ولا فضل أبو بكر بالتصديق

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha’s side cites the verse about the vision shown to the Prophet as a trial; the author says ru'ya can also refer to seeing with the eyes.
rows.anchor: واحتج لقول عائشة بقوله تعالى: وما جعلنا الرؤيا التي أريناك إلا فتنة للناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report ‘I awoke in the Sacred Mosque’ may mean that he awoke only after the journey and the sleep before it.
rows.anchor: واحتج أيضا بأن في بعض الأحاديث: فاستيقظت وأنا في المسجد الحرام وهذا محتمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author challenges Aisha’s account because she was young, did not witness the event, and did not transmit it from the Prophet; Muawiya was then a young unbeliever away from the event and likewise did not transmit it.
rows.anchor: واعترض قول عائشة بأنها كانت صغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سبحان is an indeclinable verbal noun without article, inflected forms, or a derived verb; Sibawayh says it remains indeclinable because of two added letters and proper-name status, and annexation does not make it more definite.
rows.anchor: سبحان مصدر غير متمكن لأنه لا يجري بوجوه الإعراب ولا تدخل عليه الألف واللام

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group treats سبحان as an accusative vocative, ‘O Subhan’; the author calls this weak and says it means declaring God free of imperfection.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: قال القاضي أبو محمد: نصبه على النداء كأنه قال: «يا سبحان»

rows.speaker: طلحة بن عبيد الله
rows.claim: Talha ibn Ubayd Allah asks the Prophet what سبحان الله means; the Prophet answers, ‘Declaring God free of every evil.’
rows.anchor: وروى طلحة بن عبيد الله الفياض أحد العشرة أنه قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ما معنى سبحان الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under Sibawayh’s analysis, the governing verb is one with the same meaning but not the same form; the underlying sense is ‘I sanctify God with sanctification,’ with سبحان replacing the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: والعامل فيه على مذهب سيبويه الفعل الذي هو من معناه لا من لفظه

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some exegetes say أسرى is intransitive like سرى and is linked to God by a preposition, both verbs meaning to travel by night.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم من المفسرين: أسرى فعل غير متعد عداه هنا بحرف جر تقول سرى الرجل وأسرى

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa and Ibn Masud read أسرى بعبده من الليل من المسجد الحرام, adding من الليل.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حذيفة وابن مسعود «أسرى بعبده من الليل من المسجد الحرام»

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas says المسجد الحرام means the mosque surrounding the Kaaba itself, a reading al-Tabari favors because that is the recognized meaning of the name.
rows.anchor: قال أنس بن مالك: أراد المسجد المحيط بالكعبة نفسها ورجحه الطبري

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan transmits the Prophet’s account that while sleeping in the Hijr, Gabriel and angels came to him.
rows.anchor: وروى الحسن بن أبي الحسن عن النبي عليه السلام أنه قال: «بينا أنا نائم في الحجر

rows.speaker: مالك بن صعصعة
rows.claim: Malik ibn Sa'sa'a transmits the Prophet’s account of being at the House between sleep and wakefulness; other reports place him between Zamzam and the Station, or at Shi'b Abi Talib according to Sufyan.
rows.anchor: وروى مالك بن صعصعة عن النبي عليه السلام: «بينا أنا عند البيت بين النائم واليقظان

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group takes the Sacred Mosque to mean all of Mecca, citing 48:27 and saying Mecca is the intended destination; reports from Umm Hani and the Prophet place him in her home, with one saying the roof opened.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: المسجد الحرام مكة كلها واستندوا إلى قوله تعالى: لتدخلن المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil and Qatada date the Isra to a year before the Hijra; another report from Urwa via Aisha says a year and a half, in Rajab.
rows.anchor: وكان الإسراء فيما قال مقاتل قبل الهجرة بعام، وقاله قتادة، وقيل بعام ونصف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further chronology places the journey on the seventeenth of Rabi al-Awwal, when Muhammad was 51 years, 9 months, and 28 days old; the secure limits are after the torn-page incident and before the Aqaba pledge.
rows.anchor: وقيل في ليلة سبع عشرة من شهر ربيع الأول والنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ابن إحدى وخمسين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report of Sharik ibn Numayr in the two Sahih collections saying the journey preceded revelation is a known error, as hadith scholars agree.
rows.anchor: ووقع في الصحيحين لشريك بن أبي نمر وهم في هذا المعنى فإنه روى حديث الإسراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aqsa is the Jerusalem mosque; it may be called farthest because it was then the most distant of the favored sanctuaries from the Kaaba, or simply because it was remote, stressing the night journey’s distance.
rows.anchor: والمسجد الأقصى، مسجد بيت المقدس، وسماه الأقصى أي في ذلك الوقت كان أقصى بيوت الله الفاضلة من الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing around Jerusalem consists of prophets, laws, and messengers in that region, as well as Syria’s trees, waters, and productive land; a prophetic report says the area from al-Arish to the Euphrates was blessed and Palestine sanctified.
rows.anchor: و «البركة حوله» هي من جهتين، إحداهما النبوءة والشرائع والرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘To show him Our signs’ means Muhammad saw the heavens, angels, Paradise, the Lote Tree, and other marvels; alternatively God showed Muhammad himself to people as a sign, through a vision of the heart.
rows.anchor: يريد لنري محمدا بعينه آياتنا في السماوات والملائكة والجنة والسدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All agree that the five daily prayers were prescribed for this community during the Isra.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف أن في هذا الإسراء فرضت الصلوات الخمس على هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘He is Hearing, Seeing’ subtly threatens unbelievers who deny the Isra: God hears what they say and sees their deeds.
rows.anchor: وعيد من الله للكفار تكذيبهم محمدا في أمر الإسراء، فهي إشارة لطيفة بليغة
